blocks.md: The matrix form of least squares does exactly what simple regression does, but for any number of explanatory variables at once. All the observations are stacked into one column of outcomes and one table of explanatory variables, and the whole problem of finding the best-fitting coefficients becomes a single equation that can be solved in one line. Nothing new is assumed; the notation just lets you handle ten variables as easily as one, and makes the geometry of regression visible.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Every real regression has several variables, and every result in econometrics from standard errors to instrumental variables is stated in this form.
The Classical Linear Regression Model with $N$ observations and $K$ columns in $\mathbf{X}$, including a column of ones.

sections.heading: Linearity means linear in the parameters

blocks.md: where each $f_k$ is **any** function of the data. So all of these are linear models: quadratic $\alpha + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2$, loglinear, semilog, translog, time trends, dummies, interactions. An infinite number of variations.

blocks.title: Lecture wisdom
blocks.md: Models should have a constant term unless theory says they should not.
The lecture lists four and picks one: $\sum e_i$, $\sum e_i^2$, $\sum|e_i|$, $|\sum e_i|$. Least squares takes $\sum e_i^2$; $\sum|e_i|$ (quantile/LAD regression) comes later in the course.
Each step below is one rule from [Matrix Calculus](note:matrix-calculus).

Dimension check: $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$ is $K\times K$, $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}$ is $K\times1$, $\mathbf{b}$ is $K\times1$. The derivative of a $1\times1$ scalar with respect to a $K\times1$ vector is $K\times1$.

**Second-order condition**: $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$ is positive definite under [Full Rank and Identification](note:full-rank-and-identification), so the critical point is the unique minimum ([Quadratic Forms and Definiteness](note:quadratic-forms-and-definiteness)). The lecture states the FOCs and never checks this; an exam might ask.
OLS is the sample analogue of the population linear projection. See [Conditional Mean vs Linear Projection](note:conditional-mean-vs-linear-projection).
All consequences of $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ **when $\mathbf{X}$ contains a constant**:

1. The LS residuals sum to zero.
2. The regression hyperplane passes through the point of means: $\bar{y} = \bar{\mathbf{x}}'\mathbf{b}$.
3. The mean of the fitted values equals the mean of the actual values.
None of the three holds without a constant term.
Keep these separate. It is the most common conceptual error in this material.

| Population | Sample |
| --- | --- |
| $\varepsilon_i = y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\boldsymbol{\beta}$ (disturbance, **unobservable**) | $e_i = y_i - \mathbf{x}_i'\mathbf{b}$ (residual, **computed**) |
| $\mathbf{y} = E[\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X}] + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ = conditional mean + disturbance | $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{e}$ = projection + residual |
| $E[\mathbf{X}'\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}] = \mathbf{0}$ — an **assumption** | $\tfrac{1}{N}\sum \mathbf{x}_i e_i = \mathbf{0}$ — an **algebraic identity**, true in every sample |
The right-hand column holds by construction whether or not the model is correct.
